title: Credit Cards and Debt
objective: After this level you can explain how credit card interest can turn a small debt into a big one.
summary: A credit card is revolving credit. Paying in full may avoid interest; unpaid balances compound at high rates. US statements must warn about paying only the minimum.

cards.headline: Every US credit card bill carries a warning label.
cards.body: Not about your health. Federal rules require it on every statement, and it's about one choice: paying only the minimum.

cards.headline: A loan every time you tap
cards.body: A credit card is revolving credit: you can borrow up to a set limit, then repay in one go or bit by bit. Pay the whole balance by the due date, and you may not be charged interest on purchases at all. Leave part unpaid, and that part is charged interest. It's the same card either way. What changes is whether it's working as a way to pay or as a loan.

cards.headline: The snowball, in reverse
cards.body: Level 24's snowball works on debts too. Unpaid interest is added to the balance, and then interest is charged on the lot. That's how card debt can balloon. And card rates are steep: in 2026, US card accounts charged interest paid about 22% a year on average. By the Rule of 72, a balance growing at 22% would double in a little over three years if nothing were paid.

cards.fact: The warning: pay only the minimum, and you pay more interest for longer.
cards.context: The statement must also estimate how long paying only the minimum would take to clear the balance, and what it would cost in total. It's Level 24's math, printed with your own numbers.

mascot.line: Of all the numbers on a card statement, that little box might be the most interesting one.

cards.headline: Card debt: unpacked
learned: A credit card is revolving credit up to a limit
Paying in full by the due date may avoid interest
Unpaid balances compound at high rates
Statements warn about paying only the minimum

questions.prompt: You pay your whole card balance by the due date. What happens with interest on those purchases?

options.label: You may not be charged any
You pay interest on the full amount anyway
options.rationale: Paying in full by the due date can avoid interest on purchases.

options.label: You pay half the usual rate
options.rationale: There is no half rate: paying in full can mean no interest.

options.label: The bank pays you interest instead
options.rationale: Card balances are borrowing, not savings.

questions.explanation: Paying the balance in full by the due date means you may not be charged interest on purchases; only unpaid portions are.

questions.prompt: Why can a card balance keep growing even with no new purchases?

options.label: Card companies raise the limit each month
options.rationale: A higher limit adds no debt by itself.

options.label: Unpaid interest is added and then charged interest too
Prices of past purchases are updated
Banks charge a fee for every day of the month
options.rationale: The growth comes from compounding interest.

questions.explanation: Unpaid interest joins the balance and is itself charged interest: compounding working against the borrower.

questions.prompt: In Level 23's terms, what is a credit card's rate of about 22% a year?

options.label: A tax on the shop's sale
options.rationale: It is paid by the cardholder for borrowing, not by the shop.

options.label: A reward the bank pays you
options.rationale: You pay it; it is the cost of borrowing.

options.label: A one-time fee for opening the card
options.rationale: It is charged each year on unpaid balances.

options.label: The price of borrowing the unpaid balance

questions.explanation: Interest is the price of borrowing. The card rate is what you pay each year for the use of the unpaid balance.
